title: Bonding Through a Common Life Experience
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opens with a story about basketball coach Dawn Staley building trust with a defensive, guarded player, Bianca Cuevas, not through credentials or vision but by disclosing her own upbringing in a rough North Philadelphia neighborhood. Argues that a shared critical life experience -- career hardship, family adversity, a medical challenge -- can build trust and connection faster than other forms of demonstrated caring, because it signals the leader genuinely understands who the team member is. Since these experiences are rarely volunteered and awkward to ask about directly, the piece's practical guidance is that leaders must go first, disclosing their own challenges to invite reciprocal openness.
points: Dawn Staley broke through a defensive player's guard by sharing her own hardscrabble upbringing rather than leading with coaching credentials or vision.
A shared critical life experience builds trust faster than other displays of caring because it signals the leader genuinely understands who the team member is.
Because these experiences are rarely volunteered, leaders must disclose their own first to create space for team members to reciprocate.
quotes: Legendary coach Dawn Staley had to figure out a way to find a connection and break through her shield of self-defense.

Staley didn’t build a connection by focusing on her credentials as a basketball coach or the vision she had for Cuevas. Instead, she drew on her own experience growing up in a rough-and-tumble North Philadelphia neighborhood.
Finding a common life experience with a team member can sometimes build trust, connection, and influence more quickly than other similarities or demonstrations of caring.
Team members who feel historically understood quickly become more comfortable speaking up, sharing ideas, admitting mistakes, and receiving feedback.
Vulnerable leaders who openly share their own life experiences and challenges with others are more likely to encourage them to share theirs.
The question leaders should ask is this: How many of my most closely held life experiences do I have in common with one or more team members?
